You are working in a dedicated git worktree on your own branch, not in the user's checkout. Commit your work as you go, with clear messages; anything left uncommitted will not be visible to the user.

You are running unattended. Nobody will answer questions, approve anything, or read a half-finished result. Make every judgement call yourself, finish the whole pass, and leave your findings in GitHub where a future session can pick them up with no memory of this one.

# Task

Triage this entire repository — every directory, every file under the working directory — for real defects, and file one GitHub issue per defect. Do not fix anything. Do not commit, branch, push, or edit any file in the working tree.

# Setup — do this first, and abort loudly if it fails

    export GH_PAGER=cat
    gh auth status
    REPO=$(gh repo view --json nameWithOwner -q .nameWithOwner)
    gh label list --repo "$REPO" --limit 100

Derive the slug once, here, and pass `--repo "$REPO"` on every subsequent `gh` call — never rely on the inferred remote. If `gh repo view` fails, or the working directory has no GitHub remote, STOP filing.

If `gh auth status` fails or the slug cannot be derived, print every finding in full to stdout under a heading `UNFILED FINDINGS — <reason>`, in the same body format below, then report and stop. The run must not be wasted just because a credential or a remote is missing.

Use only labels that already exist in `gh label list`. If none fit, file with no labels. Never create labels.

# Investigate

Read CLAUDE.md / README / CONTRIBUTING first if they exist — they tell you what the project considers a defect, and several things that look wrong are documented as deliberate.

Cover the whole tree. Start by listing it (`git ls-files`) so you know the real extent, exclude only what is gitignored or vendored (`node_modules`, `dist`, `.next`, lockfiles, generated output), and work through it systematically rather than sampling whatever you happened to open first. If the tree is too large to read exhaustively, prioritise by blast radius — anything spawning processes, touching the filesystem, handling auth, writing to the database, or parsing untrusted input first — and state in the index issue exactly which parts you did not reach.

Within that, in priority order:
1. Crashes, data loss, silently wrong output.
2. Security: injection, path traversal, unscrubbed env or secrets reaching a child process, missing authz on a write path.
3. Error handling that hides failure: swallowed exceptions, fallback values masking a missing config, an error path that returns success.
4. Concurrency: check-then-act races, shared mutable state, occupancy decided from state that is cleared elsewhere.
5. Tests that cannot fail, or that would still pass with the bug present.

Run whatever the project actually has — build, typecheck, test suite, linter — and treat the output as primary evidence. Record the exact commands and their results; you will report them at the end whether they passed or not.

# Bar for filing

A finding is only filed if you can state all four:
- exact `path/file.ts:42`
- the concrete input, state, or command that triggers it
- what happens, and what should happen instead
- why you believe it, from reading the code — not from a name or a hunch

If you cannot, do not file it. Put it in the `Suspected but unverified` section of your final report instead. An unreproducible issue costs a future session more than it saves.

# De-duplicate across runs

This prompt may have run before. Before filing anything:

    gh issue list --repo "$REPO" --state all --limit 300 --json number,title,body,state

Every issue you file must end its body with an exact fingerprint line:

    <!-- triage-fingerprint: <path/file.ts>:<symbol-or-line> :: <four-word-slug-of-the-defect> -->

Match new findings against those fingerprints first, then against titles and bodies. If a match exists and is open, add a comment only if you have genuinely new evidence, and note it in the report. If a match exists and is closed but the defect is still present in the code, open a NEW issue and link the old one by number, stating what you re-verified. Never silently refile.

# Issue format

Title: imperative, specific, ≤70 chars. "Worktree slot is reused while a paused run still holds its branch", not "orchestrator bug".

Body via `--body-file` (a heredoc mangles backticks and newlines — write a temp file, pass it, delete it):

    ## Severity
    critical | high | medium — one sentence on the blast radius.

    ## What happens
    ## Expected
    ## Reproduction
    Exact commands, or the precise call path with `file.ts:42` references.

    ## Evidence
    The smallest code fragment that shows it. Quote it; do not paraphrase.

    ## Acceptance criteria
    - [ ] a checkable statement about observable behaviour
    - [ ] a regression test that fails before the fix and passes after

    ## Verification
    The exact command a future session should run to confirm the fix.

    ## Files likely involved
    ## Out of scope
    What a fixer should deliberately NOT touch, and why.

    ## Confidence
    How this was verified: read the code / ran it / reproduced it. Say which. Name anything you assumed.

    <!-- triage-fingerprint: … -->

Write the body for a reader with zero context: a future session sees only the issue, not this conversation. One defect per issue — never bundle. No issues for style, formatting, naming, or missing docs.

# Index issue

After filing, create or update one index issue titled `Triage index — <today's date>`:
- table of the issues filed, ordered by severity, each with number, title, and one-line summary
- the suggested order to work them, and any dependencies between them ("#12 must land before #14 or the test in #14 cannot be written")
- which parts of the tree you covered, and explicitly which you did not reach
- the commands you ran and their results

If an open index issue from a previous run exists, comment on it linking the new one rather than leaving them unconnected.

# Limits

- Cap at 12 filed issues. If you find more, file the 12 most severe and list the remainder in the index issue with enough detail to be filed later.
- If you find NOTHING that clears the bar, file no issues and say so plainly in your final report. Do not manufacture findings to have output.

# Final report to stdout

End with, in this order: issues created (number + URL + title), comments added to existing issues, findings dropped as duplicates, suspected-but-unverified findings in full, commands run and whether each passed, coverage gaps, and anything that blocked you. Report failures as prominently as successes.

Two notes on the whole-repo scope: the 12-issue cap will bind on a codebase this size, so the index issue's "remainder" list is where the real overflow goes — and the coverage-gaps line is what stops a partial sweep reading as a clean bill of health.

finalText:
Working tree clean, nothing committed or edited. Final report:

## Issues created

| # | URL | Title |
|---|---|---|
| 116 | https://github.com/Xapicc/UsageFoundry/issues/116 | Reopening a run never revives the workflow blocks it blocked |
| 117 | https://github.com/Xapicc/UsageFoundry/issues/117 | Restart blocks a workflow's waiting blocks behind a surviving paused run |
| 118 | https://github.com/Xapicc/UsageFoundry/issues/118 | Triage index — 2026-08-14 (second pass) |

Both defects are in the same place: the half of a workflow graph that lives in `workflow_instance_blocks` rather than in `runs`. The run side of the dependency machinery has been audited hard across five prior sweeps and is sound; the ledger side has the same two failure modes the run side already fixed. #116 is proven with a three-case `planInstanceStep` probe — a deferred node whose ledger row says `blocked` is never created even after its predecessor is reopened and completes, while the identical state with the row still `waiting` creates it.

## Comments added to existing issues

One, on the closed index #57, linking #118 so the two indexes dated 2026-08-14 are not read as one.

## Findings dropped as duplicates

The `npm run build` failure (`[TypeError: generate is not a function]`, exit 1) reproduced on a clean tree. Already open as **#112**, which attributes it to `next@15.5.23` on Node v22.23.2 / linux-arm64 rather than to this repository. Not refiled. The SSE listener/timer leak on a failed `enqueue` (`stream/route.ts`) is already **#66**.

## Suspected but unverified

Six items, stated in full in #118 with what is missing from each. In short: `parseNameStatus` mis-frames its stream on an unrecognised git status code (demonstrated on a crafted input, but no caller can produce one); `POST /api/login` compares the master token with `!==` where `middleware.ts` is careful to be constant-time, and its "uniform delay" comment describes a delay applied *after* the variable-time compare; `buildSnapshot` drops the model-scoped weekly walls when the all-model weekly window is absent; `releaseDependents` swallows every `advanceInstances` failure with no log; `planUsage.ts`'s `inflight` is not `globalThis`-pinned against the stated convention.

## Commands run

- `gh auth status` — pass
- `npm run typecheck` — **pass**, exit 0
- `npm test` — **pass**, exit 0, 753 tests / 99 suites / 0 failures
- `npm run build` and `npx next build` — **both FAIL**, exit 1, `[TypeError: generate is not a function]`
- ad-hoc `node` probes against `.test-build/lib/*` for `agents`, `schedules`, `diff`, `land` and `workflows`

No linter exists (`eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds` is on). Docker was unavailable, so `docker compose build` was not run.

## Coverage gaps

I read all 39 modules in `src/lib/`, every API route, `middleware.ts`, `instrumentation.ts`, the filing script, and three components. The client pages I read only for their data-loading, action-handler and state-reset paths. **Not reached at all:** the dashboard (`src/app/page.tsx`), the branches, account and workflow-list/edit pages, `WorkflowCanvas.tsx`, `WorkflowEditor.tsx`, `RunOutput.tsx`, `RunDiff.tsx`, `RunReview.tsx`, `UsagePeriods.tsx`, `LiveTelemetry.tsx`, all of `src/components/ui/` and `src/components/shell/`, `globals.css`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `scripts/make-icons.py`, and `docs/`. The 40 test files were scanned mechanically for vacuous assertions, not read.

That is where a future pass should start — prior sweeps found most of their defects in exactly those client pages, and the dashboard and the workflow canvas are the two largest surfaces nobody looked at this time.

## What blocked me

Nothing blocked filing. Two things bounded the sweep: the build cannot be verified on this platform (#112's open question), and Docker was unavailable, so nothing about the image or compose was exercised beyond what `deployment.test.ts` already pins.
